title: What is the Kirkpatrick model?
description: The Kirkpatrick model evaluates training at four levels: reaction, learning, behavior and results. What each level measures and how to use it for compliance.
shortAnswer: The Kirkpatrick model is a four level framework for evaluating training: Level 1 Reaction (how participants respond to it), Level 2 Learning (what knowledge, skills, and attitudes they acquire), Level 3 Behavior (whether they apply it on the job), and Level 4 Results (whether targeted organizational outcomes occur). Created by Donald Kirkpatrick in the 1950s, it is a widely used structure for asking whether training actually worked.
keyTakeaways: The four levels are Reaction, Learning, Behavior, and Results.
Kirkpatrick Partners advises planning from Level 4 back to Level 1: start with the outcome, then design for it.
Levels 1 and 2 are measured most often; Levels 3 and 4 are closer to what an effectiveness question asks but are measured least.
Completion rates are not a Kirkpatrick level at all; they show exposure, not effect.
alsoKnownAs: Kirkpatrick's four levels of training evaluation

sections.heading: What are the four levels of the Kirkpatrick model?

blocks.text: The four levels measure reaction, learning, behavior, and results. Kirkpatrick Partners, the organization that maintains the model, defines them as follows ([Kirkpatrick Partners](https://www.kirkpatrickpartners.com/the-kirkpatrick-model/)):

blocks.caption: The four levels, with compliance training evidence (evidence column illustrative)
head: Level
What it measures (Kirkpatrick Partners)
Example evidence in compliance training
rows: The degree to which participants find the training favorable, engaging, and relevant
Post course survey on relevance to the role
The degree to which participants acquire the intended knowledge, skills, attitude, confidence, and commitment
Scenario assessment scores against defined outcomes
The degree to which participants apply what they learned on the job, and are supported and held accountable
The degree to which targeted outcomes occur as a result of the training and support
Fewer reporting errors, breaches, or incidents in the targeted area

blocks.text: Kirkpatrick Partners attributes the four level structure to Dr Donald Kirkpatrick in the 1950s, with later development by Jim and Wendy Kayser Kirkpatrick that added emphasis on the performance environment and on stakeholder defined return on expectations (ROE).

sections.heading: How should the Kirkpatrick model be used?

blocks.text: The model is most useful when used for planning, not only for measurement after the event. Kirkpatrick Partners states that "it is critical to start with Level 4: Results" and stresses "planning from Level 4 to Level 1 (or starting with outcomes and working backward to design for them)".

items: Define the Level 4 result the training should contribute to, and how it will be measured.
Define the Level 3 behaviors that produce that result, and the support people need to perform them.
Design Level 2 outcomes and assessment that prepare people for those behaviors.
Design the learning experience so that Level 1 reaction supports engagement and relevance.
Identify leading and lagging indicators, and collect evidence at each level during and after delivery.

sections.heading: Why does the Kirkpatrick model matter for compliance training?

blocks.text: It matters because an auditor or regulator asking whether training is effective is asking a question that completion records cannot answer. Completion records show exposure. Level 2 evidence shows learning, and Level 3 evidence shows that staff act on it, which is much closer to what an effectiveness question asks.

Research shows how rarely the higher levels are measured. A 2019 scoping review of microlearning in health professions education found that of 17 studies, 16 measured reaction, 14 measured learning, 5 measured behavior, and none measured results ([De Gagne et al., 2019](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6683654/)). See [how to measure training effectiveness](/guides/how-to-measure-training-effectiveness) and [how to show a regulator that training works](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator).

sections.heading: How is the Kirkpatrick model different from Bloom's taxonomy and ADDIE?

blocks.text: The Kirkpatrick model classifies evaluation evidence; [Bloom's taxonomy](/glossary/blooms-taxonomy) classifies the thinking a learning objective requires; the [ADDIE model](/glossary/addie-model) describes the design process. Kirkpatrick is typically applied in ADDIE's Analysis phase (to define target results) and Evaluation phase (to gather evidence), while Bloom's shapes Level 2 assessment design.

It also differs from return on investment models, which try to express results in dollars. Kirkpatrick Partners frames Level 4 in terms of stakeholder expectations and the contribution of learning within the wider performance system.

sections.heading: What does a Kirkpatrick evaluation look like?

blocks.title: Illustrative example
blocks.text: A credit provider retrains collections staff on hardship obligations. Level 4 target: fewer hardship complaints escalated to external dispute resolution. Level 3: team leaders review a sample of calls each month for correct hardship identification. Level 2: a scenario assessment requiring staff to spot hardship indicators, set at 80 percent. Level 1: a two question survey on relevance. Six months on, the evaluation reports each level and whether call review scores and complaint trends moved together.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each learning outcome and assessment point to the obligation and behavior it supports, so Level 2 results can be reported against specific obligations and connected to the Level 3 evidence an organization collects.

faqs.q: Is there a fifth Kirkpatrick level for ROI?
faqs.a: Not in the Kirkpatrick model as Kirkpatrick Partners describes it. Some practitioners add a separate return on investment level from other evaluation frameworks. Kirkpatrick Partners instead describes return on expectations and a contributive view of learning's role in results.

faqs.q: Do completion rates count as Kirkpatrick evaluation?
faqs.a: No. A completion rate shows that people were exposed to training. It says nothing about reaction, learning, behavior, or results, although it is a necessary starting point for compliance reporting.

faqs.q: Is Level 1 reaction data worth collecting?
faqs.a: Yes, but in moderation. Reaction data can flag irrelevant or confusing training quickly and cheaply. It is weak evidence of effectiveness on its own, so it should not be the main measure reported to a board or regulator.

faqs.q: How can a small team collect Level 3 evidence?
faqs.a: Start with one high risk behavior and use evidence that already exists, such as quality assurance reviews, file checks, supervisor sign off, or incident data. A small, consistent sample tied to a defined behavior is more useful than a large survey asking people whether they apply their training.
